Apple on Tuesday announced the HomeView, its biggest push into the smart home market in nearly a decade.

The new device gives Apple’s revamped version of Siri a presence in consumers’ homes, making it a critical piece of Apple’s AI strategy.

The HomeView has a 7-inch screen connected to a speaker on its base, and Apple will also sell a version that can be mounted on a wall.

It costs $299 and is available for preorder starting today ahead of its November 13 launch.

Apple has been selling its HomePod smart speakers since 2017, but those devices have failed to gain widespread traction. Amazon and Google ran away with the smart speaker market in the late 2010s, leaving the iPhone maker with just a slice of the market.

Apple only accounted for 5.2% of the smart speaker market in 2025, while Amazon accounted for 40.9% and Google was responsible for 29%, according to market research firm The International Data Corporation.

But the rise of AI assistants has sparked a renewed push across the tech industry to create devices that rely on voice input rather than typing or swiping. HomeView has a touchscreen, but Apple is also positioning it as being an easier way to talk to Siri at home without having to reach for your phone.

AI devices that see, listen and record: Are we ready for the post-smartphone world?

Siri AI on the HomeView will be able to show relevant information based on context from a users’ text messages and calendar, and Apple says it will be able to recognize up to six household members by their face. Conversations with Siri on the HomeView will also sync across devices.

Apple says data from the device’s camera and microphone are processed separately from the rest of the system so that it cannot be accessed by the device’s software, apps, Apple or the user. Content from a user’s messages or calendar only appears on the device when the user is recognized.

The device could be key in popularizing Siri AI considering Apple’s upgraded assistant only works on the iPhone 15 Pro and later. That means family members with older iPhones that don’t support Apple’s AI features will be able to try Siri AI on the new smart home device.

Apple is also promoting the device as being ideal for managing smart home devices, making FaceTime calls, listening to music and serving as a digital photo frame. Since it can recognize users, it changes the home screen’s apps and widgets depending on the person. Similar to the Apple Watch, the HomeView also has a variety of different faces for displaying information based on the users’ preferences, like calendars, photos and weather data.

The HomeView is one of several new gadgets launched under new Apple CEO John Ternus, following the debut of Apple’s first foldable iPhone last month.

Apple on Tuesday also announced a new version of the HomePod Mini, an updated Apple TV 4K with Siri AI and a collection of smart home devices designed in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric.

Apple has faced pressure to prove it can come up with a new hit product for the age of AI. Analysts have pressed Apple executives on earnings calls about whether it plans to develop new AI-powered gadgets.

Apple is part of an industry-wide race to create personalized AI assistants that consumers rely on for everyday tasks. Tech giants are preparing for a potential future in which people get things done by speaking or typing to AI agent rather than by operating apps and websites. Meta recently launched its Muse personal assistant, along with a new slate of smart glasses designed to give users easier access to its new AI helper. OpenAI is also developing several hardware gadgets.

Apple is betting that its focus on privacy and the fact that consumers already run their digital lives on its iPhones, iPads and Macs will give it an edge. The HomeView, with its ability to alter the home screen depending on who is interacting with it, follows that strategy.

But Apple has also insisted that consumers don’t need a new type of gadget to get the most out of AI, with Ternus saying at an event last month that “there’s no product in the world better designed” to be a personal hub than the iPhone.

https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/16/climate/a.markdown:
The staggering rise of AI has become a political flashpoint, especially when it comes to the data centers needed to train and operate it.

As the industry booms, many people are increasingly worried about the environmental impacts of these hulking buildings, from their seemingly insatiable demand for water and energy, to the heat and noise they produce.

Nearly 90% of Americans say they’re more concerned than excited about the rise of AI data centers, according to a CNN poll conducted by SSRS in September.

Information and statistics are flying around, with some groups framing the AI data center boom as a potential environmental catastrophe, while others say concerns are overblown or even fake . It’s adding up to a confusing picture.

So, just how bad is AI for the environment?

Go beyond the forecast with stunning stories and visuals.

Well, to be annoying, it’s complicated. The impacts of each data center depend on a slew of factors, including where it’s located, the kind of electricity that powers it and the technology it uses.

There is also a dearth of fully transparent and detailed data from AI providers, making it tricky to build an accurate picture of impacts. Instead, we rely on estimates.

To make the whole picture even more challenging, it’s difficult to project future impacts because there is so little certainty about how AI technology and demand will develop.

But here’s what we can say at the moment:

## It has big energy demands…

Training and running AI models require large amounts of computing power, and that takes a ton of energy.

AI’s energy efficiency is improving at a fast clip , but more people are using the technology and there’s been a boom in particularly energy-intensive forms.

Simple text queries, for example, typically use less electricity than a TV would over the same time period, according an analysis by the International Energy Agency. But, more energy-intensive applications, such as video generation, sometimes require thousands of times more energy. The electricity consumption of AI data centers surged by 50% last year, the IEA found.

Around 0.5% of the world’s electricity was consumed by AI data centers in 2025, according to an analysis from Our World in Data, which projects that figure will reach 1.5% by 2030.

It might sound small, but data centers are very geographically concentrated. Nearly half of their global electricity consumption happens in the United States, where data centers could account for up to 12% of electricity consumption by 2028 as AI rapidly expands, according to an analysis from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

## … and that means climate (and health) impacts

Because the world’s electricity is still dominated by fossil fuels, it adds up to more planet-heating pollution. There are big concerns that the AI boom is pushing climate targets even further out of reach .

Where a data center gets its power from is key; the more clean energy is on the grid, the lower its climate impact. Currently, global data centers are powered mostly by coal (30%), followed by renewables at 27% and natural gas at 26%.

As AI electricity demand soars, some is being met with clean energy, but there are also plenty of planet-warming fossil fuels in the mix.

Natural gas is emerging as a key data center power source in the US. The country has the most gas-fired power capacity in development globally, with more than a third intended to power AI, according to a January report from Global Energy Monitor.

Data centers are increasingly building their own energy infrastructure to avoid straining local grids and driving up people’s bills. This often takes the form of gas turbines, which are less efficient than big power plants and can not only bring hefty climate impacts but also health costs , due to harmful air pollution, including nitrogen oxides and fine particulate matter.

The public health burden of US data centers could reach $20 billion by 2028, according to one recent study .

## It’s thirsty for water

There’s an oft-cited statistic that a 100-word email generated by an AI chatbot requires about one bottle of water — just over 2 cups — to produce.

But there’s another estimate, from Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, who says the average ChatGPT query uses about one fifteenth of a teaspoon of water.

So which is right? As with many data center impacts, it depends on context and on what people choose to measure.

AI data centers use water directly to cool their equipment, but also indirectly to create the power on which they run.

The water impacts of an individual data center will depend on its specific circumstances: the technology it uses, the kind of energy it relies on and the local water situation.

Some regions, for example, have plentiful water resources; others face high stress. Around two-thirds of data centers built or in construction in the US since 2022 are in areas of water stress , according to a 2025 Bloomberg analysis.

Tech companies say they are introducing measures to slash water use, including by developing new cooling technologies. Some analysts say water concerns have been vastly overestimated and that the burger you eat or cotton shirt you wear require much more water.

But AI’s water impacts are far from minimal. US data centers could consume up to 110 billion gallons a year by 2030, equivalent to 7% of total annual consumptive use in US public water systems, according to a March analysis by scientists from the University of California, Riverside and other institutions.

Indirect water use for electricity could push this figure much higher. A recent report from Ceres, a nonprofit advocacy organization, analyzed data centers across seven states and found they used around 3.4 trillion gallons of freshwater a year for electricity generation, equivalent to roughly 12 times the annual water use of Los Angeles, Phoenix and Washington, DC, combined.

## It can be a noisy neighbor

Some of the key concerns people have about data centers revolve around quality of life impacts — including noise pollution.

Data centers can produce a cacophony of noises: the low thrum of cooling systems, the drone of gas turbines or diesel generators and the humming of equipment.

Some communities have filed noise pollution lawsuits, including residents near a huge data center in Vineland, New Jersey.

There are steps data centers can take to reduce their impact, including soundproofing equipment and the building itself. Some experts are urging state and local governments to beef up noise regulations.

## It could increase temperatures

There are also fears the data centers could create “heat islands,” warming the air and land around them — a phenomenon that would add to the temperature rises already happening due to fossil fuel pollution.

A study by scientists at Arizona State University found data center heat pollution in Phoenix warmed downwind neighborhoods by as much as 4 degrees Fahrenheit.

“Even if these data centers only contribute to an additional heat island magnitude of 1 degree or 2 degrees, that can still have a very significant impact on our lives,” said lead author David Sailor, director of ASU’s School of Geographical Sciences and Urban Planning.

More research is needed, however, to really pin down these impacts, and some experts argue there is little difference between a data center and any other industrial facility when it comes to heat.

## It’s hungry for critical minerals

One of the more overlooked aspects of AI are the minerals and metals it requires, including for semiconductors and data storage components.

Mining for these raw materials, often in the Global South, has been linked to air and water pollution, deforestation, human health risks and climate pollution.

And as AI scales and advances, it will generate electronic waste, a rapidly-growing waste stream that is toxic if not disposed of properly. Currently only about a fifth of e-waste is recycled.

There’s also concern that AI’s demand for these minerals put it in direct competition with sectors that are critical for reducing planet heating pollution, namely wind and solar energy.

## Ultimately AI’s impacts depend on us

Experts say AI’s environmental harms are not locked in. Instead, its impacts will depend on the choices we make: Where data centers are located, how they are powered, how they are regulated, how transparent AI providers must be about impacts along their full supply chains.

Before a new AI data center is built, it needs to be clear “who benefits from it,” said Kaveh Madani, director of the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health. That includes asking questions like: Does it bring jobs? Will it improve the local economy? Will it take water from local users who need it more, like farmers?

“There are trade-offs like any other technology,” Madani said. “It has has downsides that need to be regulated, monitored, and mitigated.”

CNN’s Isabelle LaBianco and Jennifer Agiesta contributed reporting.

On October 6, the Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza won the Caine Prize for African Writing, for the short story “The Blue Fighter.” Less than a week later, The Atlantic published a piece declaring that the story’s narrator “has all the personality of a chatbot.”

“The AI detector Pangram flags almost the entire story as AI-generated,” the article reported.

Kundizeza denied that he had used any such technology. “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter.’ I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work,” he wrote in a statement on X.

The Caine Prize, which comes with a £10,000 award, had become the newest front in a war engulfing the literary world, powered by AI writing tools and AI writing detectors.

Scandals about suspected AI use have spread up and down the writing industry this year. In March, the publisher Hachette canceled the US release of author Mia Ballard’s self-published 2025 novel “Shy Girl” after a New York Times report found that it may have been written using AI.

In May, a Trinidadian author named Jamir Nazir was accused of using AI to write “The Serpent in the Grove,” which won the Commonwealth Short Story Prize.

In July, researchers at Stony Brook University posited that H.M. Wolfe’s “Daggermouth,” a national bestseller, was 60% AI-written according to a data set shared with The Atlantic .

More accusations kept flying: debut author Jerry Falade lost a $2 million book deal in July after his agents pulled his debut novel over suspicions he had used AI writing tools. In September, a claim that a book by Haitian Canadian author Thélyson Orélien had failed an AI detection test led the jury for the prestigious Goncourt prize to remove him from its longlist.

As generative AI proliferates, it’s easier than ever for an author, or someone who wants to be seen as an author, to come up with a story- or book-shaped piece of text. It’s harder than ever for a reader or a prize judge or a publisher to be sure that the words on a page were produced by human thought and effort, rather than a machine prompt.

The result is a literary version of the ruined world in the movie “Blade Runner.” Anxiety and suspicion about robot infiltrators are everywhere — and so are people claiming to hunt the robots down.

Multiple companies now offer products that promise to spot the difference, with often contradictory, biased or erratic results. The makers of Pangram, an AI detection platform that has been cited as authoritative in many of the recent controversies, claim it can distinguish between human and synthetic writing with near-perfect accuracy.

“We’re trying to mitigate some of the harms that come from these powerful AI models,” said Max Spero, the CEO and founder of Pangram.

Spero is quick to admit that he doesn’t have a background in literature or creative writing. He is a machine learning engineer by trade, and worked as a software engineer at Google and an autonomous vehicle startup called Nuro before founding Pangram in 2023.

“I’m an avid reader. I’ve never been a writer. I haven’t lived in that world,” Spero said.

Nevertheless, Spero presents Pangram as a protector of the magazines and journals that make up the literary ecosystem.

“A lot of these outlets are getting flooded with submissions because they pay writers they publish and don’t charge anything to send in your work,” Spero said. “There are these perverse incentives that come from AI making it nearly free. Our goal is to help reduce the friction on the defensive side to help people understand what’s AI and what’s not.”

## What does a robot sound like?

Pangram caught widespread public attention in May, after the Commonwealth Foundation announced that Nazir’s “The Serpent in the Grove” was among the winners of its competition.

The story was ornately written, with figurative language that struck some readers as extravagant or peculiar: “Hard living lays itself on a man like wet sacking; it never asks permission. His eyes narrowed against the glare outside and the darker glare inside him: old promises that never ripened, the ache where hope should live, a gnawing sense that land can own a man while making him swear the land belongs to him.”

But many people declared they saw telltale tics of chatbot writing. A folklore has quickly grown up around generative AI prose, describing various shibboleths that are supposed to betray the robot voice.

One early AI panic revolved around the alleged overuse of em-dashes — an especially funny notion to the many magazine journalists who’d been using them for in-sentence digressions for years — while other people swear the giveaways are “It’s not X, but Y,” grandiose descriptions like “load-bearing,” or lists of three things.

The reason such devices show up in AI writing, though, is that they were already in common usage among the legions of human writers whose work AI companies ingested to train their systems.

“AI slop is sort of indistinguishable from human-written slop because the AI is trained on bad writing,” said the author Patrick Nathan. “The reason AI writes badly is because the vast majority of writing is bad.”

To back up their confidence that something was wrong with the style of the story, then, the people accusing Nazir of using AI also appealed to Pangram numbers.

“Pangram flags at 100% but also, come on, if you know you know,” Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, wrote on Bluesky. Others posted screenshots of the story’s Pangram results like trophies.

It’s not lost on the writing community that some of the most gleeful AI hunters, like the tools they use, come from the tech sector, not from among their own ranks. Readers trying to understand what was going on with “The Serpent in the Grove” could encounter Nabeel S. Qureshi, a former engineer at Palantir, posting on X about “the ‘hums’ trope, and plenty of other obvious markers of AI writing.”

## Suspicious patterns of suspicion

There’s also the glaring question of whose work gets fed into Pangram for investigation, and why. The originally anonymous accusation against Orélien was made by Samuel Fitoussi , a conservative French newspaper columnist at Le Figaro and the author of the book “Woke Fiction.” Many of the major scandals were also centered on nonwhite writers; Nazir is of South Asian descent, while Ballard, Wolfe, Falade, Kundizeza and Orélien are Black.

“Part of this has to do with a broader anti-woke and anti-Black tenor in a lot of conservative and right-leaning online discourse,” said Doyle D. Calhoun, a professor of postcolonial studies at the University of Cambridge.

Is AI rewiring your kid’s brain?

Calhoun said that for decades the literary establishment was made up mostly of white men. Now that those demographics are changing and there are more non-white authors getting book deals and winning awards, there’s an emerging resentment, especially on social media.

“Once these accusations — many of them sort of unverified or unfounded — are out there, the internet media ecosystem just goes into sort of overdrive,” he said. Historically, these sorts of claims also tend not to “stick” to white writers in the same way they do with non-white writers, Calhoun said.

Spero said that Pangram is calibrated to call something AI-assisted only if the tool is extremely confident in its analysis.

The company’s own estimates claim that false positives — in which the tool wrongly reports that a piece of human writing was created — are 1 in 10,000 and shrinking. Peer-reviewed studies from the University of Chicago and the University of Brussels support that claim, though one 2025 study from the University of Maryland found that Pangram erroneously labeled 2% of documents as AI.

A widely referenced 2023 Stanford study that found AI writing detectors produced higher rates of false positives on writing from non-native English speakers was conducted before Pangram was created. Pangram ran an internal study using a database of non-native English texts and self-reported that false positive rate was around 8 in 10,000.

## How do you prove you’re not a machine?

Prior to the emergence of AI writing tools, the cardinal sin of writing was plagiarism. But plagiarism requires two different parties and a measurable accusation. When one author steals another’s words, everyone can judge whether that’s actually the case or not. It’s not that simple with AI writing.

Publishing houses are twitchy about putting out potentially AI-written books and authors are tense about being accused of using AI to write lest they be asked to share their drafts and version history with the entire internet. Social networks are so inundated with AI writing —both real and imagined — that LinkedIn has installed a new post reaction option : “Looks like AI slop.”

Given the thousands upon thousands of pieces of writing published each day, a 1 in 10,000 chance of a false accusation — let alone an 8 in 10,000 chance — means that even the most trusted AI detector is going to be wrong, and wrong about a lot of people.

Pangram isn’t able to tell users the truth about someone’s writing, but it is able to introduce something much more complicated: doubt.

Unless an accused writer confesses to using an LLM, there is no bulletproof way to prove an accusation, short of being given full access to someone’s computer history and finding the chatbot prompts.

The Caine Prize judges said that they would using a “human centered approach” to determine the provenance of Kundieza’s story. Ellah Wakatama, chair of the Caine Prize’s board of trustees, told the BBC that the writer would send his draft history to the organization for review.

While draft version histories are not sacred texts, being asked to share them in exchange for exoneration does introduce some thorny social questions about how much writers need to show an audience — or accuser — in order to be trusted.

And once an accusation is made, there’s no consensus about what evidence would be sufficient to clear an author’s name. When Bryan Armen Graham, a sports editor at The Guardian, was accused of using AI to help him write articles, the publication called the allegations “preposterous.” That didn’t stop several others, including some journalists, from siding with the Pangram results over the word of a colleague.

## Either way, a machine wins

To some people and institutions on the literary side, using automated AI writing detectors to fight the influx of AI writing is just trading one form of technological domination for another.

Pangram has entered the public consciousness at a time of distrust that goes beyond writing. “All of this is happening in a larger milieu of bullshit,” said John Warner, the author of “More Than Words: How to Think About Writing in the Age of AI.”

The ability to dam at least some of the daily overflow of misinformation and misrepresentation is one of the reasons for Pangram’s success and adoption, but Warner said that comes at a cost.

“Like all other technology of automation, that is going to de-skill people from discerning these things for themselves,” he said.

The Commonwealth Foundation conducted a review of the work of Nazir and the other nominees, but it chose not to use Pangram or other AI detection software in the process.

“Because the tools aren’t conclusive the jury is still out as to how much they can be relied upon,” Razmi Farook, director general of the Commonwealth Foundation, said. “For us, we didn’t want to rely on a singular indicator. We believe the fairest approach is to consider multiple sources of evidence.”

Those sources, Farook said, included the original reading and judging process, along with “supporting documentation” of the writers’ “creative processes, including working drafts, notes, and other relevant materials.” There were also lengthy discussions with each author about how their stories came together.
